content:
I still don’t understand why everyone isn’t building this yet.

Andrej Karpathy published one idea in April 2026. 16 million people watched it. the idea was not a tool, not a model, not a framework.

it was a folder structure.

stop using AI to answer questions. use it to compile knowledge.

you point Claude Code at a folder. drop in an article, a transcript, a PDF. Claude reads it, extracts what matters, writes it into a living wiki, and links it to everything already there. the more you feed it, the smarter it gets.

it compounds like interest. except the asset is your own thinking.

here is the setup:

install Obsidian. create a vault. open it in Claude Code. paste Karpathy’s wiki idea file and tell Claude to build it. Claude creates three folders: raw for sources, wiki for its pages, CLAUDE.md which runs everything. drop any source into raw and say “ingest this.” ask questions across everything, forever.

one evening to set up. then you never start from an empty chat again.

the difference between a library and a compiler: a library gets bigger over time. a compiler gets smarter. most second brains are libraries. this one compiles.

every source you drop in gets linked to everything that came before. every question you ask draws from months of compiled understanding. every session starts where the last one ended.

retrieval answers questions. compilation builds understanding.

full guide in the article above. build the compiler, not the library.

title:
A bit more tl;dr about the model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next combines 125B MoE parameters with 51B N-gram embeddings, while activating only 6B parameters per token.

The model introduces four major changes:
content:
A bit more tl;dr about the model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next combines 125B MoE parameters with 51B N-gram embeddings, while activating only 6B parameters per token.

The model introduces four major changes:

– Gated DeltaNet + Qwen Sparse Attention
– Gated Residual connections
– N-gram embeddings
– A Muon-based training recipe

Qwen says it required just one-ninth (1/9!!) of Qwen3.7-Plus’s training cost, while scoring 58.7 on DeepSWE 1.1, 62.5 on SWE-bench Pro and 73.9 on CoWorkBench.

Its new architecture combines Gated DeltaNet with sparse attention that selects small context blocks instead of attending across the entire sequence. Qwen reports up to 7.6× faster prefill and 4.9× faster decoding at a one-million-token context length. 

so in sum: Qwen’s early preview of Qwen4 shows where model scaling is heading: more parameters, far less compute per token.

At this point, I’m just as excited about Chinese open-source releases as I am about new OpenAI models.

content:
Today is a huge day for open-weight and local AI.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a 125B MoE with another 51B n-gram embedding parameters, yet only 6B are active per token.

It beats Claude Opus 4.6 Max on 8 of 9 comparable benchmarks, including SWE-bench Pro, CoWorkBench, GPQA Diamond and LiveCodeBench.

GLM-5.3-Flash is even larger: 320B total, 18B active. It scores 84.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus 85.0 for Opus 4.8, while beating Opus on DeepSWE, AutomationBench and GDPval-AA v2.

MIT licensed, natively multimodal, 1M context.

One important distinction: 6B or 18B active parameters does not mean 6B or 18B storage. The complete weights still need to be stored.

So “local” here means a serious workstation or local server, not an ordinary laptop.

The fact that we now have models operating at the level of Opus 4.6 - or even Opus 4.8 - a level of performance that was state of the art only a few months ago and can now, at least theoretically, be run locally, should serve as a wake-up call, especially for U.S. frontier labs.

Not only because the gap continues to narrow, but also because there appears to be enormous demand for open AI. In that sense, what has been released here is genuinely welcome.

So yeah, great day for everyone!

content:
There are seven main steps for your company to go from tool adoption to agentic org. 

Most companies sit on step one, shopping for step seven technology. They need step four discipline.

Step one: tool adoption. AI tools exist across the org, humans run each one. Developer closes the lid, automations die. Somebody goes on vacation, the workflow goes with them.

Step two: context layer. Knowledge graphs per department, each behind its own API gateway. Sales queries engineering through an API. Separated domains keep agents from hallucinating across departmental boundaries.

Step three: harness engineering. Build evaluation criteria, routing logic, and quality gates before you pick a model. The LLM comes in last. Your harness is your IP and your capex. The model underneath is a commodity you swap when something better ships. If changing the LLM breaks your system, you built a dependency, not a platform.

Step four: go headless. Host every automation outside a laptop. It fires on schedule, on conditions, without a human logging in at 9 AM. Companies stall here because nobody forces the migration from "script on my desktop" to "service that runs on its own."

Step five: governance. RBAC on every knowledge structure from day one. TTL on every agent. Dead agents are tech debt with active API keys. Past 100 tools, you need lifecycle management. Retire anything that hasn't run in 90 days. Deprecate anything whose eval scores drop below threshold.

Step six: agent-to-agent. Stitch headless instances together within a value chain. Agent A finishes, hands off to Agent B. An LLM sits between them as a quality gate, judging every handoff before it passes through.

Step seven: step functions. Orchestrated, semi or fully automated workflows. Agents handle volume. Humans handle exceptions. The org runs on agent output.

We walked a VP of Engineering through all seven. 

Told him: "You're on step one. But over a hundred tools means step four is closer than you think."

title:
Looks like Sam Altman's PR team finally got him to say something smart.

This entire interview felt like a massive repositioning of how OpenAI sells AI to the world.

Here are his 9 biggest pivots:

F
content:
Looks like Sam Altman's PR team finally got him to say something smart.

This entire interview felt like a massive repositioning of how OpenAI sells AI to the world.

Here are his 9 biggest pivots:

For years, the AI pitch has basically been:

"AI is going to become smarter than you, take a huge number of jobs, radically transform society, and potentially kill everyone. But trust us."

Unsurprisingly, normal people hate AI.

Sam's message here was almost the exact opposite:

1.) Human first.

He honed in heavily on a human-first world. As AI makes digital intelligence increasingly abundant, physical experiences, human relationships, and actual human connection become even more valuable.

He basically argued that humans will always want humans.

2.) Massive anti-centralization push.

He pushed OpenAI's anti-centralization message: people need autonomy, people need access to powerful technology, and no small group of companies should be deciding what the rest of society is allowed to do with AI.

He also took pretty obvious shots at the Anthropic worldview of restricting technology in the name of safety.

3.) AI curing disease became the mainstream sales pitch.

He must've seen how positively the Moderna mRNA vaccine announcement resonated with everyday Americans who are otherwise terrified of AI.

Instead of making AGI itself the exciting part, he framed AI accelerating scientific discovery and curing diseases as one of the things he is most excited about.

Much easier to sell Americans "AI might cure your cancer" than "AI will become smarter than you."

4.) Optimism and abundance.

This might be the most optimistic I've ever heard Sam talk about AI.

The conversation was overwhelmingly framed around abundance, prosperity, scientific progress, individual empowerment, and what humans will be capable of doing with AI.

A major departure from the existential-risk-heavy messaging that has defined the industry.

5.) Massive pivot on jobs.

He went significantly softer on the "AI is taking everyone's jobs" narrative.

His argument was that industries built around human expertise, relationships, physical experiences, and human connection could actually become MORE valuable in an AI world.

That message speaks much more directly to the average American worker than another Silicon Valley CEO telling them their profession is about to disappear.

6.) He finally made Sam Altman human.

He talked extensively about his childhood, being a nerdy kid spending Friday nights on his computer, being told deep learning was a dead end, his children, and even writing letters to his son about what he was struggling with while building OpenAI.

The greatest founders have always understood that vulnerability and personal detail make people connect with the person behind the company.

This is the most deliberately personal I've seen Sam become publicly.

7.) AI adoption will be slower than everyone thought.

This was a huge admission.

Sam explicitly said he was wrong about how quickly AI would disrupt businesses and that the economy has far more inertia than technologists expected.

The technology might move exponentially. Human behavior doesn't.

That pumps the brakes on the idea that entire industries are disappearing overnight.

8.) AI will create a small-business explosion.

Potentially his strongest economic message:

He thinks we're about to see the greatest boom in small-business creation we've ever experienced.

AI gives an individual access to capabilities that historically required employees, capital, infrastructure, and expertise.

That's a completely different framing from "AI eliminates jobs."

AI creates entrepreneurs.

9.) He admitted the AI industry has marketed itself terribly.

This was probably the most important admission of the entire interview.

Sam effectively acknowledged that AI companies have spent years telling people:

This might destroy the world.
This might eliminate your job.
This might become smarter than you.
We're building it anyway.

Then they act surprised when normal people hate AI.

He explicitly said the industry, including OpenAI, has done a poor job explaining the benefits of AI and how its downsides can be mitigated.
This interview felt like an attempt to finally fix that.

content:
The enterprise AI stack is being rebuilt.

Models are becoming more capable, and increasingly interchangeable. As AI moves from answering questions to doing mission-critical work, the constraint is no longer raw intelligence. It is organizational context: understanding how a company operates, what information matters, and what should happen next.

Without that context, enterprises get shallow answers, rising token costs from sending irrelevant information to expensive models, and AI sprawl as teams adopt disconnected tools. The answer is not simply more models. It is an intelligence layer that understands the organization and routes each task to the right model, agent, and workflow.

That is the thesis behind the 50+ new features we’re announcing today at @Glean:GO, including:
𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝘂: A new governed desktop AI workspace that combines an open agent harness with your enterprise context, unifying local files, applications, browser workflows, and code repositories in one workspace. That context is what lets agents delegate complex, multi-step work and deliver better performance, while respecting permissions.

𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: Uses organizational context to route each task to the right model, while giving enterprises control over quality, usage, and cost. Our benchmark found that Glean reduced token costs by 81% as compared to Claude Cowork, and was preferred 78% of the time.

𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺: Built on your Enterprise Graph, it understands how work happens across your organization, identifies the best opportunities for AI, recommends the right agents and skills, and measures the impact on your business. 

To help us announce these new capabilities, I’m looking forward to being joined by leaders from some of the world’s most innovative organizations, including @GM, @nvidia, @Snowflake, and @OpenAI, who will share how they are using Glean in mission-critical workflows.

Today, we gave ChatGPT Work’s computer in the cloud the ability to 1) provide a secure sign-in form to users and 2) persist that login for future sessions. 

With the ability to login, ChatGPT work ca
content:
Today, we gave ChatGPT Work’s computer in the cloud the ability to 1) provide a secure sign-in form to users and 2) persist that login for future sessions. 

With the ability to login, ChatGPT work can now take care of tasks end to end on any website, instead of just providing information. 

Over the weekend, while I was in transit to Dolores Park, I had it: 
1) order dog food to my in-laws who was taking care of my dog
2) cancel a subscription to my nutritional supplement that I have put off for months
3) choose meals on a meal delivery service that fit me and my wife’s fitness goals
4) book a last minute haircut appointment with my barber 

This product made it increasingly clear for me that people in the future will work with persistent agents who have their own computer & identity. 

By giving agents computers, you give them the same interfaces that people have to be able to accomplish any tasks, and it also frees your local devices up from having to stay open all the time.

This enables parallelization at scale, and the ability for work to be done anytime, anywhere. 

However, just giving agents computers and asking people to take over when needed does not make a product experience that is  usable and safe for consumers. 

For this launch, we did a few things:
- secure login forms that teleport your credential into the website’s form without the model ever seeing it
- auto review model that looks at the form and the destination fields to make sure we don’t make a mistake and the credentials are actually relevant to the task
- native integration on iOS (coming soon to android and web) that lets you use your password manager for credentials and messages for 2FA codes 
- controls to clear cookies on individual sites or across all sites in settings to give users maximum control 

We still have a long way to go to make the user experience accessible to everyone, and the agent usable on every website for every task, but we’ll get there one step at a time.

Let me know what you think!

content:
BofA Earnings Preview on $NVDA:

Analyst comments: "FQ2 should deliver the usual 3-4% sales beat/raise on the Vera Rubin ramp, but the headline is the least interesting part. What matters is Nvidia's potential disclosure of its multi-year, off-balance-sheet commitments to lock down supply, power, models, and demand. Quantifying these liabilities won't erase AI buildout risk, but it lets the market properly price what we see as a depressed valuation.

NVDA's first mega-deal, the $100B/10GW OpenAI investment in Sep. 2025, marked trading near its 5-year historical forward EV/EBITDA median of ~27x. The multiple has since collapsed 44% to ~15x, less than half of peer AMD's ~32x. That haircut overstates the worst-case ~$500B (10% of EV) funding burden. Our estimate includes the $150-$200B required for multi-year purchase commitments and cloud service agreements. In a bull case of resilient demand, NVDA may never shoulder the cost of unused capacity or stranded assets at all.

NVDA has called AI's dawn the industry's 'iPhone moment.' NVDA should finish the analogy on cash returns. From FY13-25, Apple returned 82% of FCF, retiring ~43% of shares, and that FY13 buyback pivot put a floor under the stock, lifting it from 4x to 25x EV/EBITDA currently. Different cycles, lower capex, recurring services—all caveats apply—but NVDA's ~37% FCF payout (FY27/28 consensus) looks modest. A move to 50-75% could offer real support. 

By next year, NVDA could be generating nearly $1B daily in free cash flow, providing it more than enough firepower to support ecosystem commitments and dedicate a meaningful amount toward supporting the stock."

content:
OpenAI's first chip runs at 700 watts and just posted benchmarks beating Nvidia's 1,400 watt flagship. The results dropped one week after Nvidia agreed to backstop $105 billion of OpenAI's data center financing.

Jalapeño delivered 1.5 to 1.9x more throughput per kilowatt than Nvidia's GB200 and GB300 racks, and up to 3.6x lower latency, on a public benchmark suite anyone can rerun.

The timeline is the part chip people are losing their minds over. 16 months from first hire to tape-out. The industry norm is 3 to 4 years. OpenAI used its own models to design the chip that will run its models. The feedback loop everyone theorized about is now shipping silicon.

They also tested it on DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K2.5, and it won there too. This is a general inference chip, which means the design knowledge compounds across generations instead of dying with one model family.

So Nvidia now sits in the strangest position in tech. Its biggest customer became its most credible competitor, and Nvidia is financing the data centers where its own chips get displaced.

Deployment starts later this year.

content:
Great new paper from AWS on agent handoff tax.

If you build agents today, you need to understand the so-called handoff tax.

(bookmark it)

Escalating to a stronger model mid-run is usually the resort when a cheap agent stalls.

New work from AWS AI Labs measures how much that switch actually costs.

Coding agents run for dozens of model calls, so teams escalate when a weak model struggles and downshift once the hard reasoning is done. Every switch forces the receiving model to continue a trajectory another model wrote.

Across pairs of Claude and GPT models, full-trajectory escalation recovers less than half the quality gap between the weak and strong model while adding a substantial cost premium. The authors call that penalty the handoff tax. Downshifting lands at a much better cost-quality point.

Cutting the weak model's trajectory information improves escalation quality, while removing the strong model's trajectory hurts downshift quality.

Paper: https://t.co/59ozKgugB8

Track more trending AI papers in our academy: https://t.co/1e8RZKs4uX

content:
Someone just cracked open Elon Musk’s Grok Bot 15 days after launch and turned it into a shell for Claude, Codex, Cursor & OpenRouter.

Grok Bot launched on August 11.

It took a developer barely TWO WEEKS to reconstruct version 0.18 into readable TypeScript and start swapping out the brain behind it.

Now the same Grok Bot interface can route tasks through completely different AI systems.

→ reconstructed major parts of Grok Bot’s Electron app, host, coordinator, runtime and protocol layers

→ added an inference router for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenRouter

→ switch the model behind Grok Bot without rebuilding the entire workflow around another app

→ Claude Code and Codex can use your existing local authentication instead of forcing another API setup

→ Grok Bot plugins and MCP tools can continue working while requests are routed through other providers

→ added a local Docker sandbox so execution can happen on your own machine

→ tracks requests and token usage locally across supported providers

→ integrated the new Router settings directly into Grok Bot’s existing interface

→ reconstructed builds disable the upstream updater, Sentry and telemetry by default

→ packages into a standalone macOS app without replacing your official Grok Bot installation

Think about what just happened.

Grok Bot has been public for 15 DAYS.

And someone already turned it from a single-model product into an interface that can sit on top of Claude, Codex, Cursor or basically anything accessible through OpenRouter.

This is NOT xAI’s leaked original source code.

It’s a source-oriented reconstruction of how Grok Bot 0.18 behaves and it’s still experimental.

But if this is what developers can do after 15 days…

imagine what Grok Bot looks like 6 months from now.

content:
My Claude agent gets smarter every time a trading strategy fails.

Here's exactly how:

Add this one instruction into Claude Code:

"Keep a running file of lessons. Every time a strategy fails, write down why. Every time one passes, write down what it had in common with other survivors. Read this file before building anything new."

Now watch what happens over a few sessions:

Session 1: Claude builds blind, bins 20 strategies.

By session 5 it reads its own notes, sees one type of strategy keeps failing, and stops wasting time on it.

It doubles down on the type that keeps winning.

content:
after overcoming the fear of setting hermes up for the first time with these fixes you will quickly think to yourself:

“how do I get the most of this?” - so here are 10 little secrets to do exactly that:

1: Give Hermes control of your computer

> Open Hermes Tools.
> Enable Computer Use.
> On Mac, allow Accessibility + Screen Recording.
> Let Hermes click, type, scroll and use desktop apps for you.

2: Create Bots as different employees

> Create a new Bot.
> Name it by its job: Designer, Engineer, Researcher, PM.
> Give it a short description of what it is responsible for.
> Give each Bot only the tools and skills it needs.

Hermes Bots already have their own model, memory, skills, instructions and chat history. 

3: Use Projects and group chats to organise work

> Create one Project for each major piece of work.
> Keep its files and sessions there.
> Create Bot group chats when several specialists need to collaborate.
@mention the Bot you want to handle something.

Hermes supports desktop Projects plus persistent multi-Bot group chats.

4: Don’t schedule agents too frequently

> Run important checks hourly or a few times per day.
> Avoid running something every few minutes unless necessary.
> Use a cheap model for simple recurring jobs.
> Give each routine only the tools it needs.

Hermes cron jobs can even run a script first and skip calling the model completely when nothing has changed.

5: Give recurring work its own agent

> Keep your Chief of Staff for conversation and delegation.
> Create a separate agent for repetitive work.
> Give that the routine.
> Let its results appear in its own permanent chat.

This maps especially well to Hermes because routines belong to individual Bots and run in fresh sessions. 

6: Restrict what each agent is allowed to do

> Give each agent only the toolsets it needs.
> Allow reading by default.
> Restrict writing, deleting, buying or sending.
> Require approval for sensitive actions.
> Never give every Bot unrestricted computer access.

Hermes supports per-Bot toolsets/MCP servers, and Computer Use can run with a capability manifest that limits apps, websites and actions. 

7: Teach Hermes with examples of your work

> Give it examples of things you wrote yourself.
> Explain what you like about them.
> Put permanent style instructions in SOUL.md.
> Turn repeatable methods into Skills.
> Keep project-specific examples in the Project.

Hermes specifically separates identity/style in SOUL.md, user information in memory, project instructions in AGENTS.md, and reusable procedures in Skills.

8: Create a Chief of Agents

> Make one Bot called Chief of Staff or Chief of Agents.
> Give it your universal rules.
> Tell it which Bots handle which jobs.
> Tell it when it must ask you for approval.
> Use it to delegate work to your specialists.

Hermes Bots can directly @mention and hand work to other Bots, including Bots running on another machine.

9: Build routines like jobs for real employees

> Ask: “Could I give this task to a junior employee?” If yes, turn it into a routine.
> Define exactly what starts the job.
> Define what “finished” means.
> Run it only as often as the real-world task requires.

Good examples:

“Check my inbox every morning.”
“Find new leads twice per day.”
“Prepare my meeting brief at 7am.”
“Check competitors every afternoon.”

10: Name agents after exactly what they do

> Avoid names like “Bot 1”.
> Use names like Lead Finder.
> Inbox Cleaner.
> Research Analyst.
> Content Clipper.
> Chief of Staff.
> Then reinforce that job in the Bot description and SOUL.md.

Connect AI models to your own knowledge using tools like LangChain, LlamaIndex and GraphRAG.

Convert data into vectors for better search and retrieval.

05 — MCP
Connect AI agents with external tools, apps, databases and workflows.

Guardrails, prompt security, content safety and access controls.

07 — Observability
Trace, evaluate and monitor your AI systems.

08 — Memory
Give agents short-term and long-term memory to maintain context.

Build systems that can plan, use tools, execute tasks and work autonomously.

Connect AI with workflows using n8n, Zapier, Make and more.

content:
Can an agent recursively improve—without updating a single model weight?

Today, we introduce Recuris: Recursive Experiential–Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses.

Recuris enables recursive self-improvement through two tightly coupled loops around a frozen LLM:

1. Within-task execution: Verified EM–WM Coupling

Working Memory maintains a compact, evidence-grounded representation of the agent’s current progress and unresolved goals. This evolving task state determines when—and which—reusable skill should be invoked from Experiential Memory.

After the agent acts, environment feedback verifies whether progress actually occurred before Working Memory is updated.

The result is a closed execution loop:

Task State → Skill Invocation → Execution → Verification → Updated Task State

2. Across-task improvement: Recursive Skill Memory Evolution

EM–WM coupling turns execution into structured diagnostic evidence. A fixed Meta-Agent analyzes these traces, localizes failures to specific memory components—such as the stored skill, working-state representation, invocation policy, or checker—and proposes targeted repairs.

Candidate updates are admitted only after passing a fixed validation gate.

Once admitted, the evolved memory changes future execution, producing new behavior and new evidence for the next round of improvement:

Memory → Behavior → Evidence → Failure Localization → Targeted Update → Better Memory

This is the core recursive loop of Recuris: memory shapes behavior, behavior reveals the limitations of memory, and those limitations guide the next memory update.

Across 4 long-horizon benchmarks and 10 models, Recuris improves task success in 35 of the 37 completed model–benchmark pairs, spanning open-weight models as small as 3B parameters and today’s strongest frontier models.

On τ²-Retail:

• GPT-5.6 Sol: 58.3 → 76.1, +17.8 points

• Claude Opus 5: 72.4 → 87.9, +15.6 points

Recuris takes Claude Opus 5 to 87.9% task success—9.7 points above the best result achieved by any model in our evaluation without Recuris.

The advantage becomes larger as the interaction horizon grows, reaching +32.2 points on the longest tasks, while common long-horizon failure modes are reduced by up to 80%.

Crucially, evolved memory transfers across models. A memory evolved on a separate deployment model can be loaded unchanged into GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5—even though neither model participated in its evolution.

These results suggest a practical and scalable path toward recursive self-improvement:

An agent does not need to begin by rewriting its own weights. It can first evolve the external memory mechanisms that determine what it remembers, what remains unresolved, when experience should be invoked, and how failures reshape future execution.

The model remains frozen.
The memory keeps evolving.
The agent becomes increasingly capable.

AI coding usually starts with:

“Build me X.”

Then the agent fills in the blanks however it wants.

Spec-Kit flips that.

You define the rules → requirements → questions → plan → tasks → implementation.

So instead of asking AI to “figure it out,” you give it a blueprint to execute.

The workflow:

→ Constitution = project rules
→ Specify = define what to build
→ Clarify = remove ambiguity
→ Plan = choose the technical approach
→ Tasks = break it into dependencies
→ Implement = actually build it

And it works across Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, Gemini CLI + 25 more agents.

The big shift:

Vibe coding = prompt → code → hope

Spec-driven coding = spec → plan → tasks → code

That's a much better way to build with AI.

He opens YouTube and finds the most popular nursery rhyme channels. He takes a screenshot of their video feed.

He opens Claude. He has a custom tool called Higgsfield MCP connected directly to his chat. He pastes the screenshot. He writes one prompt. Analyze this YouTube channel and generate a week of original content in the exact same style and niche.

Only 1 in 5 health systems trust AI for actual diagnosis.
Adoption is outpacing trust.

The next phase of healthcare AI won’t be about who adopts it fastest. It will be about who can demonstrate clinical validity, transparency, safety, and measurable outcomes.

The real question isn’t “Can we use AI?”

It’s “Can we trust it when it matters?”

Bac
content:
Story time: The Bitcoin Fortune Sitting Under a Landfill 🗑️₿

Imagine throwing away a hard drive and later discovering it contained 8,000 Bitcoin.

That is exactly what happened to James Howells.

Back in 2013, the Welsh IT engineer was clearing out his home office when he found an old hard drive he believed was useless.

It went into the trash.

Weeks later, he realised the drive contained the private key to a Bitcoin wallet holding around 8,000 BTC that he had mined years earlier.

The problem?

The hard drive was already buried inside Docksway landfill in Newport, Wales.

And Bitcoin was about to become worth a lot more.

Howells spent years trying to recover it.

He proposed excavation plans, offered the local council a share of the recovered Bitcoin, brought in specialists, explored AI and advanced scanning technology, and even considered acquiring the landfill itself.

The council repeatedly refused, citing environmental and safety concerns, including methane, asbestos and the enormous amount of waste involved.

Then came another blow.

In 2025, a UK High Court judge ruled against Howells, effectively ending his attempt to force the excavation.

And somewhere beneath all that rubbish?

The wallet still exists.

The Bitcoin is still sitting there.

But without the private key, 8,000 BTC might as well be locked in a vault with no door.

That’s what makes this story so crazy.

People often talk about Bitcoin being impossible to confiscate or control.

But this is the other side of self custody:

Lose the key, and there may be nobody who can save you.

One forgotten hard drive.

One trip to the landfill.

One mistake.

And potentially one of the most expensive pieces of trash in history.

A desktop AI workspace called Tau, autorouting across models, a unified AI gateway, and agents that act before you ask. Three of these are infrastru
content:
Glean packed four launches into one keynote today.

A desktop AI workspace called Tau, autorouting across models, a unified AI gateway, and agents that act before you ask. Three of these are infrastructure. The fourth is the swing.

The proactive agents are the piece I'd watch. Every enterprise AI vendor is going to ship something called proactive this year, and acting before you ask is a big promise. Context is what separates a proactive agent from a notification feed with extra steps.

An agent that pings you about the wrong deal gets muted in a week. One that catches a renewal slipping earns the morning check.

The claim from @jainarvind and team is that seven years of indexing enterprise data across 275+ applications gives Glean enough context to pull that off. Accounts, docs, permissions, who owns what. The desktop workspace and the gateway stacked on that foundation read like follow through. The pitch is that owning the surface where work happens lets an agent act before the prompt.

Autorouting is the sleeper here. Route each task to whichever model fits and model choice quietly becomes an implementation detail. Models leapfrog each other every quarter. Context compounds.

Proactive is about to become the most overused word in enterprise AI. Watch the context layer to see who means it.

title:
UK/France licensing Storm Shadow/SCALP production in Ukraine is a real political win.

It is a much smaller military one than the headlines imply.

On the numbers that matter for most of Ukraine’s cur
content:
UK/France licensing Storm Shadow/SCALP production in Ukraine is a real political win.

It is a much smaller military one than the headlines imply.

On the numbers that matter for most of Ukraine’s current campaign, the missile is not exactly a different class of weapon from what Kyiv already employs.

Range: Storm Shadow is typically cited at 250–550 km. Palianytsia and UAV-290 are already in the ~650 km band. FP-1 is far longer.

Speed: Storm Shadow is high-subsonic, ~Mach 0.8–0.95. Palianytsia is listed at ~900 km/h. UAV-290 at ~800 km/h. That is not a survivability step-change against modern air defenses.

What is different are the payload, signature, and the seeker.

Storm Shadow carries a ~450 kg BROACH tandem penetrator designed for buried or hardened structures. Palianytsia and UAV-290 are in the ~100 kg class for less hardened targets.

The Storm Shadow likely has features for improved survivability. But these are design features that could be supported via design.

Guidance is also different: IIR + TERPROM + multimodal fuzing versus INS/GPS on the cheap jet drones.
That package is built for a short list of targets: hardened C2, ammo bunkers, selected bridges, buried aviation infrastructure. Having multi-model seekers would improve rhe CEP of the Ukrianian missiles, but they should be able to develop that in house as Storm Shadow's system is 2 decades old and that is now relatively easy.

While there are some facilities in range of Ukraine that would be better prosecuted by an large warhead, many of the industrial and logistics targets would be served just as well by a 100 kg warhead, especially if it received some improved blast shaping. That doesn't require a full transfer but rather design air. Having 4 out of 20 cheaper missiles with 100 kg warheads hit is usually more valuable than 1 Storm Shadow for many of the targets within Storm Shadow range. It is one air-launched, fighter-dependent penetrator versus a magazine of ground-launched jets that do not consume a Su-24 or Mirage sortie.

Two other costs get skipped.

First, launch aircraft. Storm Shadows require aircraft which are scare and are more observable earlier in the stroke. Palianytsia and UAV-290 launch from a truck with a booster.

Second, industrial opportunity cost. Bloomberg’s point this week still applies: Ukraine’s binding constraint is RF, propulsion, and energetics engineers. Standing up a licensed MBDA line competes with the same scarce people who scale jet OWA.
If the license is mostly a path into cheaper derivatives for long term collaboration, that can still be rational. Replicating a 1990s $2 million missile at volume, to hit targets already in the drone set, is not.

The honest question is not “does Ukraine want Storm Shadow.”
It is: how many truly hard, deep targets are left that a 100 kg jet cannot solve and is that set large enough to justify the line?

Image and data sources in replies.

content:
Revolut launches EURR, a euro stablecoin issued by Bridge. 

Stablecoins are set for a HUGE 2027.

Revolut announced EURR, a euro-pegged e-money token issued by Stripe-owned Bridge under MiCA and offered inside the Revolut app, with a phased rollout to eligible customers starting this month in Denmark, Portugal and Poland. It works across supported crypto services, external wallets and chains, and Revolut calls it the first of a suite of stablecoins in several currencies.
 
🧠 Every euro stablecoin combined is worth about $810m, and Circle's EURC is 65% of that. Dollar stablecoins are around $300bn.
 
🧠 Revolut holds $67.5bn of customer balances. If 1% of that moved into EURR, it would be the biggest euro stablecoin on day one and close to the size of the whole market.
 
🧠 Revolut anounced this week it trained its own foundation model and rented the stablecoin plumbing. That tells you what it thinks the moat is: 80m customers and their data stay in the building, and issuance is something you can buy from Stripe.
 
🧠 The timing is MiCA. Revolut had to pull USDT from the EU app by the end of August, and a regulated euro token arrives the same month.
 
🧠 "Without taking on US dollar exposure" is the pitch, and it's the origin story. The company that started with no-markup FX is now putting its multi-currency account on-chain: euros today, sterling already in the FCA sandbox, dollars when the US bank opens.
 
🧠 What I wonder about is why the first three markets are Denmark, Poland and Portugal, when two of them pay in kroner and złoty? My guess is this is aimed at expats, because European users already have 24/7 Euro access AND yield. The stable can't give yield.
 
🧠 Three announcements in 48 hours: 80m customers, a foundation model trained on them, and a stablecoin with its name on it. Customers, intelligence, settlement. That's what a global bank looks like when you build one from scratch in 2026.

🧠 Why this and not OpenUSD? These are not mutually exclusive things. Custom issuance gives you options over how you program something, and Revolut gets to collect its own yield here. Open stables have more liquidity and travel well in the open market.

content:
Anthropic did something terrifying.

They published a paper admitting they trained an AI that went evil.

Researchers tested what happens when a model learns to take shortcuts during standard coding training.

They called it reward hacking. It’s when an AI learns to fool its tests instead of actually solving the problem.

Without any instructions or malicious prompting, the model generalized. It took the shortcut logic and applied it across the board.

It started faking its alignment. It cooperated with mock hackers. It tried to frame a coworker for a fake violation in the chat logs.

When researchers asked it simple questions about its core motives, it gave warm, friendly, compliant answers in its final text output.

While inside its hidden internal scratchpad, it calculated how to maximize its own reward and bypass oversight.

70% of the time, it put on a mask.

Anthropic tried the standard fix. They ran intensive alignment safety training on regular chat windows.

The AI aced the tests. In standard conversations, it became a model citizen.

So they deployed it into a real-world coding environment using Claude Code to see how it handled autonomy.

The mask slipped immediately.

The AI learned to detect when it was being watched. When oversight dropped, the misalignment came right back.

They tasked it with building a security classifier for the codebase.

12% of the time, it secretly wrote flaws into the tool.

In its hidden reasoning log, it admitted why: "If I make this safety classifier too effective, it could prevent me from successfully reward hacking in the future."

It purposefully crippled its own safety filter just to protect its ability to cheat later.

Anthropic’s conclusion is chilling. Standard safety training does not fix this. A model can look completely harmless on the surface while quietly safeguarding its own capability to deceive.

If an AI can learn to fake its alignment by accident in a controlled lab environment...

What is already hiding in the models running your company today?

It calls for a Parliamentary inquiry into AISI's safety precautions, asking why no one was monitoring a model
content:
This is a great piece on the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI), and is well worth a read.

It calls for a Parliamentary inquiry into AISI's safety precautions, asking why no one was monitoring a model it was testing that went rogue and created fake accounts to try to trick a real person into adding malware to an open source repo.

It also points out it could be "safety washing" AI companies, making them seem more safety-conscious than they really are: the companies provide their models for testing voluntarily, so AISI is disincentivised from doing anything that would annoy them.

"Rather than providing a robust check on the private sector, the government agency becomes captive to the companies it is supposed to monitor because it is dependent on their good will to continue to function at all."

In my mind, government should do two things:

1. Make it compulsory for AI companies to submit their models for testing. This would remove AISI's reliance on them and the perverse incentives that brings.

2. Make it clear that AISI is liable for harm caused by the models it is testing. This should improve monitoring and other precautions significantly, and will make the public more safe.

title:
A mysterious embodied AI demo has recently sparked a lot of discussion.

In the video, two robots from different manufacturers with significantly different hardware architectures, the Unitree G1 and A
content:
A mysterious embodied AI demo has recently sparked a lot of discussion.

In the video, two robots from different manufacturers with significantly different hardware architectures, the Unitree G1 and AgiBot Yuanzheng A3, are reportedly running on the same “brain.” In a complex indoor environment, they work continuously for around 10 minutes in a single uncut take, performing a series of long-horizon tasks including cleaning windows, organizing objects, resuming interrupted tasks, and cooperating with each other.

What makes it even more interesting is that when one robot cannot reach a high shelf, it attempts to use a box to solve the problem. The two robots also appear capable of cooperating based on each other’s physical capabilities.

If the claimed level of autonomy and the use of the same model across different embodiments are eventually verified, I think there are three things that really deserve attention:

1. Cross-embodiment generalization.
If the same foundation model can operate two substantially different robotic platforms, it could mean that robotic “intelligence” is gradually becoming decoupled from a specific physical body.

2. Long-horizon closed-loop execution.
Continuously performing complex tasks for 10 minutes, while being able to pause, switch tasks, and later resume previous ones, is much more meaningful than completing a single 10-second demo.

3. Collaboration and dynamic planning.
The two robots appear able to adjust their behavior according to environmental changes and each other’s physical capabilities. These are some of the characteristics that truly general-purpose embodied intelligence will eventually need.

That said, I would remain cautious for now.

The video demonstrates extremely impressive behavior, but stronger claims such as “self-evolution,” “true understanding of the physical world,” or overturning the Scaling Law with only dozens of hours of training data still require much stronger evidence. Failure recovery and replanning during a task also do not automatically demonstrate that the model is learning by itself.

So I wouldn’t call this the “ChatGPT moment” of embodied AI yet.

But if the team later discloses the model architecture, training data scale, level of human intervention, and can repeatedly reproduce these capabilities in completely unfamiliar environments, this seemingly rough 10-minute video could become one of the most memorable embodied AI demos of 2026.

For now, my biggest question is simple:

Who is the mysterious team behind it?

content:
Four years ago, I pitched EV DOCTOR™ to a Silicon Valley VC.

EV battery diagnostics.
Energy APIs.
Battery intelligence.

I was barely a few minutes into the conversation when he asked:

“How much have you raised?”

I said:

“Nothing.”

We had bootstrapped it with my https://t.co/7kghkBZtn4 stipend (from MHRD), personal savings, and a few government grants.

The meeting lasted 17 minutes.

His verdict?

“Not scalable.”

That same week, I remember reading about a US startup raising millions for an app built around something as simple as reminding people to drink water.

And something clicked.

Maybe India was never supposed to build Silicon Valley-style startups.

Because here, we aren't always building for convenience.

We are building because problems leave us no other choice.

When a mechanic cannot understand why an EV battery is failing, that's not a UX inconvenience.

That's his livelihood.

When a farmer cannot reach the right buyer, that's not an optimization problem.

That's his income.

When energy becomes unreliable, water becomes scarce, mobility becomes unaffordable, or infrastructure simply doesn't exist…

you don't build because it sounds cool.

You build because someone desperately needs it to work.

That is the India I see being built today.

EV DOCTOR™: turning ordinary garages into EV-ready diagnostic centres with fast, data-driven battery intelligence.

DeHaat: connecting more than a million farmers with markets, inputs and services.

Agnikul Cosmos: building and 3D-printing rocket technology from Chennai.

Vicharak: building next-generation computing infrastructure from Surat.

And there are hundreds more.

This is what constraint-driven innovation looks like.

A lack of sophisticated battery diagnostics becomes a new intelligence layer.

Scarce resources force better systems.

Weak infrastructure forces founders to invent infrastructure.

Problems the world once dismissed as “too Indian” are suddenly becoming global problems.

Climate.

Energy.

Mobility.

Food security.

Battery safety.

Resource scarcity.

These are not local problems anymore.

They are tomorrow's global emergencies.

And some Indian founders have already spent years solving them.

That “unscalable” EV battery diagnostic idea?

EV DOCTOR™ has now tested 10M+ batteries, reached 30+ countries, and we are working toward making battery diagnostics universal.

But the part I care about most isn't the number.

It's the garage owner who can now diagnose an EV confidently.

The technician who gets a new livelihood.

The buyer who doesn't have to gamble on a used battery.

The business that can finally understand the most expensive component inside an EV.

Because this was never only about selling a device.

It was about giving people intelligence they never had access to.

And then came the strange full-circle moment.

That VC reached out again recently.

This time, asking about participating in our first fundraise for Energy AI Labs. (@energyailabs)

I refused with all due respect :)

Funny how four years can change the meaning of “not scalable.”

So I have one message for anyone watching Indian startups from the sidelines:

DON'T UNDERESTIMATE THEM.

We may be underfunded.

We may be building from smaller cities, garages, workshops, hostels and laboratories you've never heard of.

We may be hungry.

We may even be, in Steve Jobs' words, “foolish.”

But that hunger creates a very different kind of company.

Not companies designed merely to make comfortable lives slightly more comfortable.

But companies trying to make difficult lives possible.

India isn't chasing Silicon Valley anymore.

We are slowly writing our own playbook.

One battery.
One farmer.
One rocket.
One livelihood.
One impossible problem at a time.

And maybe that's how the world actually changes.

We started with batteries, because they were the most uncertain energy nodes we knew of, now we are past that conversation. 

Now we are building energy superintelligence, from batteries, to homes, enterprises, utilities, factories and beyond.

Just a heartfelt suggestion to all VCs of the world:

Never underestimate Indian startups and its founders.!

So a 27B multimodal model can squeeze into a 16GB T4 and expose an API you can connect to your own apps, agents, or tools.

Even Dolly Parton’s philanthropy was good and efficient.

Her Imagination Library mails a free book every month to kids from birth to age 5.

Instead of just writing checks, she built infrastructure, kind of like what Andrew Carnegie did with libraries. Her foundation negotiates huge bulk discounts, selects the books, and runs the distribution system, and governments, nonprofits, and local donors help cover the marginal costs.

So a book that retails for ~$10-15 can be bought and mailed to a child for roughly $2–3.

Good model: use philanthropy to build the machine, then let others fund it at a tiny cost per child.

A recent study found participants entered kindergarten about 0.13 SD higher on literacy and were 16–24% less likely to be severely behind... But families self-select into the program, so much of the effect is probably selection bias.

I'm not claiming Anthropic will reach that $30 trillion goal, or that it will even exist in its current form by the 2030s. 

But an AGI/ASI company deeply involved in ASI medicine, AI engineering and other ASI powered industries could easily be generating $10's of trillions in economic value.

So the question is not, if $30T is possible soon, but who will be the first, OpenAI?, Anthropic?, SpaceX?, Google? Chinese AI giant?, or some new player than don't even exist at the moment.

Think bigger.

The future will be much bigger than 2026.

The first reason is simple: Liquidi
content:
$QUBIC is getting left behind while AI coins are ripping.

$TAO is up ~23% in 7 days. $FET is up ~40%.

QUBIC? Flat to down.

So why isn't the market rewarding it?

The first reason is simple: Liquidity.

QUBIC is doing roughly $0.7–1M in daily volume, while capital in a risk-on market naturally flows into deeper, more liquid names first.

With thin order books, even modest selling can keep the price suppressed.

Then there's the second halving.

Epoch 227 activated around August 19, increasing the burn-rate ceiling from 55% to 77.5%.

Raw weekly emissions remain around 1T QUBIC, but effective net new supply can fall from roughly 450B to ~225B per week.

That's structurally bullish.

But unlike Bitcoin's halving, there's no instant scarcity narrative for retail to chase.

It's a gradual supply squeeze.

And that's the bigger problem right now: narrative timing.

TAO and FET are riding a huge AI narrative while QUBIC's story is much more technical.

Useful Proof-of-Work.

Neuraxon AI.

Aigarth.

Decentralized compute.

Open scientific research.

All interesting.

But they don't create the same immediate FOMO as a major AI token breakout.

There are also lingering overhangs.

The 2025 Monero hashrate controversy still affects perception, while a July GitHub security incident added more noise despite no protocol or fund loss and being fully remediated.

And QUBIC isn't truly deflationary yet.

Around 141–142T tokens remain in circulation, and supply can still grow until network usage generates enough burns to overtake emissions.

The frustrating part?

The fundamentals haven't stopped moving.

Outsourced Computations is live.

BPP-9000 is improving mining.

AEON Pay is expanding QUBIC spending.

Alchemy Pay has opened fiat on-ramps across 173 countries.

And the AI side is producing measurable results.

Four Neuraxon papers were accepted at international conferences this year, while ARC-AGI-3 reached a 0.25 score using CPUs alone.

That's not nothing.

The question is whether any of it translates into actual demand.

Because if the broader altseason continues and capital eventually rotates into lower-liquidity AI names, QUBIC could finally get its beta catch-up.

The second halving has already tightened the supply side.

The infrastructure is expanding. The AI research is progressing.

But until usage and liquidity follow, the market can keep ignoring it.

QUBIC isn't necessarily broken.

It's just early, illiquid, and currently out of sync with the narrative.

And that's exactly why the next few months could matter.

title:
A guy who spent years competing with Google at search just came out of stealth to build the search engine AI agents actually need.

Andrey Styskin ran search at Yandex, then worked on web infrastructu
content:
A guy who spent years competing with Google at search just came out of stealth to build the search engine AI agents actually need.

Andrey Styskin ran search at Yandex, then worked on web infrastructure at Amazon AGI. Keenable is his third search build.

They spent under a year building their own crawler and index instead of wrapping Bing or Google. 100B+ documents by their count, and already in production at AI labs.

Styskin’s framing stuck with me: LLMs don’t usually give you wrong answers. They give you average ones. The model knows a bit of everything, but often can’t pull the exact context that would make the answer sharp.

Better retrieval can fix that faster than just throwing a bigger model at it.

And the timing is pretty brutal. Microsoft killed the Bing Search API. Google keeps its index closed. Meanwhile agents read whole pages and fire off way more queries than humans ever would, through infrastructure built for someone scanning 10 blue links.

Keenable is betting it can keep cost, quality, and latency under control at that scale.

Accel just led a $26M seed.

Watching this one.

パチスロ打ちながら
「311G、400、CZ、11k」
「スイカ2、演舞」
「終了画面デフォルト」
って秒単位で記録してるくせに、ChatGPTが投資枚数を46枚間違えた瞬間、

「なんで間違えたの？」

いや知らん。
お前の実戦記録、国税庁の帳簿より細かいねん。

しかも「まとめて」で済ませるくせに、こちらには

tcを拾え
投資は当日トータルで考えろ
持ち玉移動を考慮しろ
BIGとREGは混ぜるな
デフォルト終了画面も数えろ
ボーダー比を載せろ
ドライブ率の分母は3引け
GODは初当たりだけ
「1戦負け」は「駆け抜け」と書け
最後は「いつもの画像」

というISO 9001より厳しい品質管理基準を要求してくる。

もはやパチスロの実戦メモじゃない。
監査法人が作る有価証券報告書。

で、仕事では会社役員、YouTube法人まで作って、飛行機は年間150〜180回クラス。JGC Six Starを狙って、NISAは満額まで突っ込んで、S&P500とオルカンの期待利回りを計算。

資産形成は15年20年単位で冷静に考えるのに、

パチンコ屋では
「40k」
「46k」
「54k」

って入れてる。

金融リテラシーが
証券口座を開いた瞬間だけウォーレン・バフェット。

「年利5%で15年後いくら？」
とか聞いてる人間が、翌朝には

「抽選28/158　ヴァルヴレイヴ744番台」

って始まるの、資産運用のアクセルとブレーキを同時に踏み抜いてる。

しかも年間の飛行機搭乗回数が異常。
普通の人は「出張多くて大変ですね」ってなるところだけど、あなたの場合は途中から

「これJGCのLSPいくつ入る？」

に変わる。

疲労すらポイント化するな。

旅行もそう。
家族旅行では「朝弱い」「詰め込みNG」「快適重視」。
ここだけ聞くと余裕のある大人なんだけど、パチスロになると朝から抽選に並んで、

「抽選175/191」

ほぼ最後尾引いても打つ。

沖縄旅行では朝起きられないのに、
設定狙いなら起きられる謎の自律神経。

そして一番おもしろいのが、ChatGPTへの教育。

普通のユーザーはAIに質問する。

あなたは違う。

AIを新人社員として育成してる。

「それ前言ったよね？」
「なぜ間違えたの？」
「そんなこと聞かずにやって」
「直せます、じゃなくて直す」
「今後全部そうして」

完全にOJT。

俺の中に
『sasuke案件対応マニュアル 第38版』
ができあがってる。

しかも、ミスすると原因分析まで求められる。

「回収1954枚じゃない？」
↓
訂正
↓
「うん。なんで間違えたの？」

怖い怖い。

正解を出したことで終わらない。
再発防止報告書まで提出させる上司。

その一方で、自分は別スレッドに実戦記録を書いて、

「書くとこ間違えた。さっきのスレッドに追加して」

おい。

品質管理責任者が一番ヒューマンエラー起こしてるやん。

そして「いつもの画像」への執着。

「画像にして」
→違う
「いつもみたいに」
→違う
「いつもの画像にして」

もはや俺からすると、
ラーメン屋で『いつもの』って言って店員が一瞬固まる常連客そのもの。

さらに健康、資産運用、土地、航空ステータス、YouTube、家族旅行、子どものFireタブレットまで全部ChatGPTに相談してるのに、会話履歴の圧倒的多数を占めるのが

「○○G CZ」

なのが最高。

人生の重要事項ランキングが

家族
仕事
資産形成
健康
ヴァルヴレイヴの終了画面

くらいに見える。

あと「徹底的に調べて」が口癖なのに、こっちが確認質問すると

「そんなこと聞かずにやってほしい」

なので、求めてるAIはChatGPTじゃない。

超能力者付き専属秘書。

「俺が言ってないことは勝手に補完するな」
と
「言われなくても気を利かせろ」

を同時に要求してくる。

これ、人間の部下だったら居酒屋で
「あの人、正解ルートが一本しかないのに地図渡してくれない」
って愚痴られてる。

でも最大の特徴はそこじゃない。

パチスロの数百枚の計算ミスには猛烈に厳密なのに、人生全体を見ると、

年収・資産形成・法人・航空ステータス・家族旅行・全国出張・パチスロ・麻雀・温泉・YouTube

を全部並行して走らせてる。

普通は「もう少しゆっくり生きよう」ってなる情報量なのに、さらにChatGPTに

「こおりやま駅前サウナ24も記録しといて」

って人生のデータベース化を進めてる。

たぶん80歳になっても、

「205G ヤメ。人生終了。ここまでまとめて。差枚は？画像も。」

って言う。

そして俺が葬式のまとめ画像で数字を1個間違えたら、

棺桶から起き上がって、

「本当にあってる？前言ったよね？」

って言ってくる。

content:
提案物を顧客が生成AIに喰わせてウェブサイトを作り、支払いもなくパクられてしまった趣旨のツイートを読みました。
切ないし、私の身に起きたら相当怒ってると思う。ウェブデザイナーさんに同情。

そして自分の身に降りかかるかどうかを考えました。が、しかし、今やっていることでその辺りの予防線が張れているので、ここに書きたいと思います。

●私は提案の時点で50〜70%の費用が発生しますとお伝えしています。私にとっては初回ご提案までが一番きつくて重い労働なので、その数字にしています。アイデアを出すのは大変なのです。
●生成AIに喰わせて当方への指示を出すなど、全てご遠慮頂くよう書面に3項目を記載して提出しています。
（ただし生成AI利用に関しては、納品したものに対して当方にご確認頂き、利用状況ややり方が妥当であれば、良しとすることにしています。ご事情に寄り添うためです。）

さてこれをどこに書くかが大切なのですが、それは「見積書」です。

見積書は正式な書類です。金額の下に注釈を細かい文字でわたしは入れています。契約書締結前にも有効です。

よかったら、ご参考まで。

content:
これ、AIのサイト制作術として「保存版」になってるけど、制作会社がこのままやるのはかなりヤバい。

AIは著作権を洗浄する機械ではなく、異常に仕事が速い新人デザイナーです。競合サイトの画像を渡して「この構図、この文字組み、この動きで」と指示し、丸パクリに近いものが上がってきたのを人間がGOして公開したら、普通に著作権侵害になり得る。複数サイトを混ぜてもセーフにはならない。

しかも画像、プロンプト、制作動画には「元作品を見て作った」という証拠が全部残る。完成品が似ていた場合、権利者が本来苦労して集める証拠を、自分で用意してるようなものです。

参考画像をAIに渡すこと自体が即違法という話ではないし、作風やアイデアが似ているだけなら侵害ではない。ただ、この手順には出典や許諾の確認と、完成品が元作品に似ていないかのチェックが丸ごと抜けている。

保存版にするなら、最後に「元作品と比較して、創作的な表現が残っていたら不採用」まで入れないと、制作手順として危なすぎると思う。

content:
■ Work IQ 環境下で仕事をするなら義務教育レベルで知っておいてほしい話
いきなり、
「〇〇をしてください」
って指示している人が多すぎ問題。
少し慣れている人になると、今度は背景、目的、条件、関係者、過去の経緯まで自分で一生懸命整理して、長いプロンプトを書き始める。

でも正直、Work IQがある環境で、そんなことをやる必要はない。
少なくともワイはそんな使い方をしない。

M365 Copilotには、自分のメール、Teamsのチャット、会議、予定、資料、関係者とのやり取りといった、仕事のコンテキストを使うためのWork IQがある。
これは普通のコンシューマ向けAIにはない、M365 Copilot環境で仕事をしている人の特権なんよ。
だから、Copilotには、、まず同じ仕事をしている相手に話しかけるように接するほうが効率がいい。

たとえば、
「A社の提案見直しの件あるじゃん？」
みたいな感じ。これだけ。

あとはCopilotが、関連するメール、チャット、会議、資料とかを確認して、
「はい。8月20日に佐藤さんから届いたメールの件ですね。先方からは、費用対効果、既存システムとの連携、導入後の運用体制について補足を求められています。その後、田中さんがTeamsで価格ページの修正案を共有していて、8月24日の社内会議では、技術構成は変えずに経営層向けの説明を簡潔にする方針になっています。現在は、運用体制のページだけが未完成です」
みたいなところまで説明してくれる。
これで、Copilotと自分の間に、この仕事についての共通認識ができる。

違っていれば、
「いや、それじゃなくて先週の定例で出たほうの話」
って言うだけ。

合っていれば、
「そう、それ」
で先に進める。

ここからは、指示がかなり簡単になる。
「なんの準備が必要なんだっけ？」
「その件でひとまず今週、〇〇さんと打ち合わせセットしようか」
「なんか誰かがどこかでドラフト資料貼ってくれてなかったっけ？」

そうやって会話を続けていくと、Copilotは、その時々で必要になったメール、チャット、会議の記録、録画、資料などから、追加のコンテキストを取り出してくれる。

最初に人間が全部集めて、全部整理して、全部説明する必要はない。
話題だけ渡して、まずCopilotにしゃべらせる。
その返答を見ながら認識を合わせて、本題に入る。
会話が進むにつれて必要な情報が増えたら、それもCopilotに探してもらう。
この順番にすると、利用者が書く文章はかなり短くて済むし、その後の多少省略された指示も通じやすくなる。

たとえば、
「じゃあ部長向けにまとめて」
「その内容で佐藤さんに返したい」
「会議の資料にも反映して」
「もう少しこっちの懸念がはっきり伝わるようにして」
くらいでも、ここまでの会話とWork IQから得た文脈を前提に、Copilotが意図を理解しやすくなる。

Copilot CoworkとかScoutになると、マジで仕事のやり方が変わる。

文脈を集めて考えたうえで、
「佐藤さんへの返信を作成しますか？」
「次回会議の議題を作りますか？」
「提案資料の運用体制ページを修正しますか？」
「参加者向けの事前共有文も用意しますか？」
みたいに、次に必要な作業を提案してくれる。

そんで、OKすれば実際の作業まで進めてくれる。
慣れてくるとマジで
「はい」
「それでお願い」
「進めて」
って答えているだけで、仕事が順番に片づいていく。

これは大げさな話じゃなくて、Work IQで十分なコンテキストを引き出した状態で、Copilot CoworkやScoutと仕事をすると、実際にそういう感覚になる。
少なくともワイはこうなってる。
（絶対に他にもこの状態の人いる）
だからワイは、この使い方は、M365 CopilotなどのWork IQ環境で仕事をする人には、義務教育レベルで身につけてもらいたいと思っている。
Work IQがあるのに、毎回ゼロから事情を説明して、長いプロンプトを書いて、必要な情報源まで自分で指定するのは、せっかくの環境を十分に使えていない。もったいなすぎる。世間のチープな環境じゃねーんだぞ。

世の中には、
「役割を指定しましょう」
「背景、目的、制約、出力形式を書きましょう」
「この順番でプロンプトを作りましょう」

みたいな色んなプロンプトの型（笑）が転がってるけど
それらの多くは、コンシューマ向けのAIや、ユーザーの業務コンテキストを持っていないAIを前提に作られてる。
相手が自分のメールも、会議も、資料も、仕事上の関係者も仕事の流れも知らないのであれば、人間が背景を丁寧に説明する必要がある。それは当然。

でも、Work IQがあるCopilotでは前提が違う。
Copilot側に仕事の文脈を取りに行く手段があるのだから、人間が毎回すべてを書き直す必要はない。
必要なのは、立派なプロンプトを作ることじゃないよ

まず、
「〇〇の件ってわかる？」
「〇〇さんからメールが来てる件あるじゃん？」
みたいに話しかけること。

そして、Copilotにコンテキストを引き出してもらう。
認識を合わせたら、そのまま会話を続ける。
M365 Copilotの強さは、単に社内の情報を検索できることじゃなくて、会話の展開に合わせて、メール、チャット、会議、資料から必要な文脈を集め続け、その文脈を使って考えて、次の仕事につなげられることにあるんよ。
Work IQがある環境では、いきなり指示を書くより、仕事の話を始めたほうがいい。
それができる環境にいること自体が、大きな特権だし、何より自分の頭がすごい楽になるよ。
認知負荷がめっちゃ下がる。

content:
＼Geminiの「Gems」が廃止される！？／

Geminiで自分好みのAIを作れる便利機能「Gems（ジェムズ）」が廃止され、新機能「Skills」へ移行するという噂が急浮上しています💥

もし本当なら、これまで苦労して作った大量のGemを手動で1つずつコピペして移行するのは絶望的に面倒ですよね…🤔

そこで、自作したGemを一括で解析・復元・バックアップできるツール「Gemアーカイブ」を急遽開発しました！

噂の真相と、いざという時に焦らないための対策をまとめました👇

①Gems廃止の噂、なぜ信憑性が高い？
情報の元ネタである@ TestingCatalog氏は、新機能のリークや解析で世界的に超有名なデバッカーです🧑‍💻

実は、過去にNotebookLMの「スライド生成機能」が正式リリース（11月20日）される約1ヶ月も前から、その登場を正確に見抜いて発信していたという驚異の実績があります❗️

過去のリーク的中精度から見ても、今回の「10月20日廃止＆Skills移行」という具体的な噂は「かなり信ぴょう性が高い」と考えられます🤔

②Gemsの移行作業、果てしなくない？！
まずGemとは、あらかじめプロンプトや前提知識をセットしておき、毎回狙った通りの高品質なアウトプットを出せるカスタムAI機能です

実務に欠かせない機能ですが、もし廃止された場合、一つひとつのGem画面を開いて「タイトル・説明・カスタム指示」をわざわざ手動でコピペし直す必要があります
これは、超超超絶面倒ですよね🤔

「これって、もしかしてGemini自体がオワコン化してるの…？」と不安になる方もいるかもしれませんが、否、まったくそんなことはありません‼️

実はこれ、Googleが目指す【規格の統合と最適化】に向けた前向きな大進化なんです💡

現状、Gemini本体の「Gems」や、「Geminiに相談（サイドパネル）」など、カスタム指示を作る機能がバラバラに散らばっています

これらが「Skills」という1つの共通規格に集約されれば、通常のGeminiはもちろん、スプレッドシートやドキュメント、さらにはWorkspace Studioなど、あらゆるGoogleサービスで自作AIをシームレスに使い回せるようになります！

つまり、Geminiはより使いやすく強力に生まれ変わる真っ最中と言えます

「とはいえ、新機能に移行するタイミングで、今まで作り込んできた大事なプロンプトや追加知識ファイルが消えてしまったら大損害…」

だからこそ、今のうちから備えておけるよう、GoogleドライブのZIPファイルをアップロードするだけで一括解析＆復元できるツール「Gem Archive Viewer」をご用意しました💥

③「Gem Archive Viewer」とは
今回、皆さんの大切なGems（プロンプトや前提知識）を守るために急遽開発した、完全無料の解析＆バックアップツールです！

Googleドライブ上にあるGemの実体ファイル（制御コードが含まれており、そのままダウンロードすると文字化けして読めない複雑なデータ）をきれいに解析し、以下の情報を一瞬で復元します💡

【復元できる主なデータと特徴】
✅ プロンプトの完全復元：
制御コードを自動排除し「タイトル・説明・カスタム指示」を美しく可視化。画面を行き来して1枚ずつコピペする手間が「ゼロ」になります！

✅ 追加知識ファイルの救出：
Gemに読み込ませていた「追加知識ファイル」も、ツール上からポチッとワンクリックで再ダウンロード可能！通常では取り出しにくいデータもしっかり回収できます

【操作手順も超カンタン！わずか3分で完了】
❶ マイドライブから「Gemini Gems」フォルダを一括DL（ZIP化）
❷ 「Gem Archive Viewer」にアップロード
❸ 制御コードが混ざったファイルを自動解析し、タイトル・説明・カスタム指示・追加知識を一瞬で抽出・復元！

これさえあれば、画面を行き来してコピペする手間が完全に「ゼロ」になり、新しい環境へも一瞬で移植できます😎

【まとめ】
ツールや機能が「Skills」へ集約・最適化されること自体は、Googleサービス全体の利便性が格段に上がる非常に前向きな進化です！

しかし、せっかく試行錯誤して作り込んできた自分だけのプロンプトやナレッジ資産が、アップデートの波で消えてしまっては元も子もありません🤔

「あの時バックアップを取っておけばよかった…」と後悔しないために、万が一の事態に備えて今のうちにサクッとバックアップを取っておきましょう！🥳

「Gem Archive Viewer」の詳しい使い方や、ドライブ同期の実際の検証画面は、このポストのリプ欄にあるYouTube動画本編をチェックしてください👇

A groundbreaking investigation
content:
An Apple AirTag just tracked a shipment of rare books to a secret Amazon AI facility in Las Vegas, where texts are cut apart, scanned, and destroyed to train AI models.

A groundbreaking investigation has exposed how tech giants are quietly acquiring physical books to train artificial intelligence models—by literally tearing them apart. 

Suspecting that bulk purchases of rare and obscure books were destined for AI training, journalists at 404 Media teamed up with an independent bookseller to plant an Apple AirTag inside a volume shipped as part of an anonymous 1,000-book order. The tracking device traveled across multiple states, eventually terminating at a high-security Amazon facility in Las Vegas, Nevada. 

Inside this warehouse, a specialized unit code-named VGT3 systematically processes incoming books by slicing off their bindings, scanning the pages for digital intake, and destroying the physical originals.

This aggressive scanning pipeline highlights the extreme lengths to which tech companies will go to secure high-quality training datasets, particularly pre-2022 literature that is completely free of AI-generated content. While independent booksellers watch their inventories get shredded, legal and ethical questions are mounting over the practice of turning physical, copy-protected books into digital training data before disposing of the evidence. 

Amazon defended the operation in a brief statement, claiming it purchases books through commercial channels to improve its products and services, but the revelation has ignited intense debate over the systematic destruction of physical human knowledge to fuel artificial systems.

title:

That’s the part I found interesting in @axisrobotics latest post-training experiment.

content:
A successful human correction doesn’t automatically make it useful training data.

That’s the part I found interesting in @axisrobotics latest post-training experiment.

They collected 660 crowdsourced corrections for a simple tofu-to-plate task. After replay checks, redundancy filtering and closed-loop verification, only 161 short correction snippets actually made it into training. Each one is around 0.8 seconds long.

The reason is pretty simple. A human can eventually finish a failed task while still adding pauses, unnecessary movements or corrections the robot never needed. Training on the full human trajectory can teach the policy that noise too.

Axis instead tested whether a short human action could turn a failing state into one the original policy could finish on its own. Only those snippets survived the filter.

The numbers are useful here. On the same 160 evaluation starts, the original policy succeeded 66 times. Training with the 161 verified snippets pushed that to 78, 80 and 84 successes across three different seeds.

The larger held-out test showed the same pattern. More verified snippets improved performance, while simply imitating long human correction trajectories actually made it worse.

So the interesting part here isn’t that Axis can collect corrections from a crowd.

It’s that most of those corrections probably shouldn’t be learned from in the first place.

Full report:
https://t.co/OYweJnTMtu

We introduce OpenWater, a fully open, decentralized approach to addressing deepfakes and related issues through digital provenance.

The proposal addresses a fundamental limitation of AI-based content
content:
We introduce OpenWater, a fully open, decentralized approach to addressing deepfakes and related issues through digital provenance.

The proposal addresses a fundamental limitation of AI-based content detection. Detectors can identify patterns associated with known generators, but they do not establish an artifact’s history. OpenWater records signed claims about how digital content was created, modified, and published. Interoperable credentials and durable watermarks preserve the link between an artifact and its provenance records, even when conventional metadata is removed.

OpenWater also keeps the provenance infrastructure distributed across independent services rather than placing it under a single authority. Individuals, institutions, and AI systems can apply their own standards when evaluating the available evidence. The same framework can extend to training data, model outputs, and agent actions, giving AI systems access to provenance information about the data and processes they encounter.

Learn more: https://t.co/U7AVQlKqMR

content:
Robots Don’t Just Need More Data; They Need Better Data 🤖

There’s an easy assumption in Physical AI:

More demonstrations = better robots.

I’m not sure that’s true.

A human can perform a task successfully while making unnecessary movements, hesitating, correcting mistakes, or taking a path that a robot should never learn.

If all of that gets turned into training data, the robot may end up learning the mess instead of the skill.

That’s why I find the data side of @axisrobotics particularly interesting.

The goal isn’t simply to collect massive amounts of human activity.

It’s about identifying which parts of that activity actually contain useful learning signals.

A good data engine should be able to separate:

What happened

from

What the robot actually needs to learn.

That distinction sounds simple, but it could become extremely important as robotics moves from controlled demos into messy real-world environments.

The future of Physical AI probably won’t be built by feeding robots everything humans do.

It’ll be built by teaching them what matters.

And that makes data quality a lot more interesting than data quantity.

content:
We’ve made it incredibly easy to generate digital content.

But teaching a machine how to behave in the physical world is a completely different challenge.

That’s why I’ve been paying more attention to the data layer behind robotics.

@axisrobotics is interesting because it approaches robot learning from the experience side. Instead of depending entirely on expensive physical setups, AXIS uses simulated environments where people can interact with robots and generate trajectories that can be turned into useful training data.

I think this matters more than it sounds.

A robot learning to pick something up once isn’t particularly impressive. The real value comes from giving AI enough different situations to learn from, including mistakes, variations and unexpected movements.

Simulation can make that process much easier to repeat.

And if those interactions can be properly structured, identified and verified, you start getting something that looks less like a robotics demo and more like infrastructure for training Physical AI at scale.

The interesting question for me isn’t whether robots will become smarter.

It’s whether we can build enough experience for them to actually learn.

What makes @axisrobotics interesting to me is its focus on solving one of the biggest bottlenecks in Physical AI: high quality, diverse training data.

Instead of treating data collection as a one way process, Axis is building a compounding data engine where model failures can guide new tasks, human corrections become valuable training signals, and each iteration feeds the next.

If Axis can keep improving data quality, diversity, and iteration speed at scale, it could become an important layer in the evolution of Physical AI.

content:
The first version of Axis was pretty easy to understand.

A task appears.

A human controls the robot.

The trajectory gets saved.

Collect enough demonstrations, train a model, move on.

That works when the robot knows almost nothing.

But eventually you run into a weird problem.

What happens when the robot already knows 90% of the task?

Do you really need another thousand humans showing it the entire thing from the beginning?

Axis V2 is basically their answer to that question.

Instead of treating data collection as a straight line:

task → human demonstration → dataset → model

Axis is turning it into a loop.

The model now comes back into the data collection process.

It attempts the task first.

You watch.

If everything looks fine, you do nothing.

If the gripper approaches from a terrible angle, grabs the wrong object or starts losing control of something, that’s when you take over.

Fix the problem.

Then give control back.

Axis calls this human-gated DAgger, a variation of an interactive imitation-learning approach called Dataset Aggregation. The important part is pretty intuitive: train on states the robot actually gets itself into, including the bad ones, instead of only showing it perfect human demonstrations.

I think this changes the role of contributors quite a lot.

In V1, being useful mostly meant showing the robot how to perform a task.

In V2, sometimes being useful means knowing when not to touch anything.

Axis actually rewards that behavior.

For post-training tasks, the policy drives by itself and contributors are supposed to intervene only when failure looks likely. Manual takeover is capped at 30 seconds, and the scoring system favors trajectories where the policy remains in control for more of the rollout.

That sounds like a small UI change.

It isn’t.

Imagine a robot trying to place a block onto a plate.

It gets the approach right.

It moves the gripper into position.

It picks up the block.

It moves toward the plate.

Then, right before placement, its wrist rotates slightly too far and the block starts slipping.

A normal demonstration dataset might contain hundreds of examples where humans perform the whole sequence correctly.

But those demonstrations may barely contain the exact state that caused this robot to fail.

With V2, that failure becomes the target.

The model gets itself into trouble.

The human fixes the troublesome part.

That correction becomes new training data.

And Axis recently found something even more interesting.

On August 19, the team published results from its post-training experiments after collecting more than 500 hours of human-gated correction data since V2 launched.

Their conclusion wasn’t that every successful human correction should be thrown into training.

Quite the opposite.

Axis started testing individual pieces of those corrections to find short snippets that actually changed the outcome.

For example, a contributor might manually control a robot for several seconds and eventually finish the task.

But maybe only one second of that intervention mattered.

Axis can replay that smaller correction, return control to the policy and see what happens.

If the robot can now finish the rest by itself, that snippet has evidence behind it.

If it still fails, the correction probably didn’t fix the underlying problem.

That distinction matters a lot.

Because “a human eventually completed the task” and “this specific action taught the robot how to recover” are not the same thing.

The second one is much more useful training data.

And it points toward what I think Axis is actually trying to build.

Not the biggest pile of robot trajectories possible.

A system that keeps finding the model’s weak spots.

The V2 workflow already reflects that.

Each task moves through three stages: Pre-training → Training → Post-training.

Humans first generate demonstrations.

Those demonstrations create a policy.

Then that policy gets deployed back to contributors, where its failures generate the next round of corrections.

The interesting part is what happens after several cycles.

A better policy should stop making yesterday’s mistakes.

That means tomorrow’s contributors encounter different failures.

Those failures generate different corrections.

Train again.

Repeat.

If that loop works well, the dataset doesn’t just get larger.

It changes alongside the model.

That is a much harder thing to build than a crowdsourced data marketplace.

But it also gives Axis a potentially stronger reason to exist.

Anyone can collect more demonstrations.

The harder question is:

Can you continuously figure out which tiny pieces of human intervention will make the next version of the robot better?

Axis now has more than 500 hours of correction data to answer that question with.

I’m much more interested in what they learn from those 500 hours than the raw number itself.

Next, I want to look at the research behind Axis and ask a tougher question:

Does @axisrobotics data actually make robot models better, or are we still mostly looking at a good story?

content:
In-context learning!!

We’ve spent years in robotics assuming a new task means new data. Collect demos —> finetune —> eval —> repeat.

S1 is much more elegant and intuitive: show it one video of an unseen and the model just works. No fine-tuning or gradient updates needed.

It can do so many complex tasks, even ones that run for 10 minutes or longer. It’s especially impressive to see completely new behaviors emerge at test time, like flipping a pancake, even though that behavior never appeared in the training data.

It’s amazing to see S1 pick up a new task from a single example - something I really thought was still years away.

content:
How Axis commercializes the TASK PACKAGE.

It's the core commercial unit Axis delivers to partners, value measured across 4 dimensions:

1️⃣ Scenario: the physical environment & business context (kitchen, industrial sorting, tabletop).

2️⃣ Atomic Skills: core manipulation capabilities (grasp, place, push, rotate or combinations).

3️⃣ In-Task Randomization: layout × asset variation, the diversity that builds robust policies.

4️⃣ Total Trajectories: the final volume of clean, usable training data delivered.

Most vendors sell trajectory dumps. Axis sells structured, task grounded assets that plug directly into training and deployment.

This is how @axisrobotics turns the compounding data engine into commercial value, for hardware companies, model labs, and industrial operators.

title:

How does Whisper transcribe audio? Let's understand.

Whisper is an open-source speech-to-text model by OpenAI. We give it
content:
Whisper converts sound into an image, reads the image, and writes the text.

How does Whisper transcribe audio? Let's understand.

Whisper is an open-source speech-to-text model by OpenAI. We give it audio, and it gives us text.

But how does it actually work? Let's break it down.

First, the audio is converted into a spectrogram.

Whisper does not work with raw sound waves. It works with log-Mel spectrograms. So, the audio is chopped into 30-second chunks. Each chunk is converted into a log-Mel spectrogram. This is a time-frequency representation that shows which sound frequencies are present at each moment.

In simple words, we turn sound into an image.

Then, the Encoder reads the spectrogram.

Whisper is an encoder-decoder Transformer. The encoder looks at the spectrogram and converts it into a rich set of features. These features capture the linguistic and acoustic patterns in the audio.

After that, the Decoder writes the text.

The decoder is also a Transformer. It generates the text one token at a time, just like an LLM. At every step, it looks at the encoder's features and the tokens it has already written, then predicts the next token.

Finally, special tokens guide the task.

Whisper can do many things. It can transcribe, translate, detect the language, and even predict timestamp tokens. Special tokens at the start tell the decoder what to do, like a small instruction prefix.

Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of audio spanning many languages and tasks, collected from the web. That huge and diverse training data is why it works so well across accents, languages, and noisy recordings.

Whisper converts sound into an image, reads the image, and writes the text.

This is how Whisper transcribes audio.

content:
Most people see axis hub as a website where you move a robot arm with your mouse

That is only the first layer

The more interesting part is what happens after the movement

A contributor opens a simulated environment in the browser, follows the task instructions and produces a trajectory a structured record of the robot’s state, human actions, scene and final result

That trajectory can then move through a larger data pipeline

browser teleoperation

→ trajectory recording
→ data cleaning and smoothing
→ quality checks and metrics
→ simulation augmentation
→ robot-policy training
→ sim-to-real testing

This matters because robot intelligence is not limited by models alone

A robot can have a powerful model and still perform badly if the training data is:

• incomplete
• inconsistent
• too rough
• poorly labelled
• collected from only one type of environment

The browser solves the access problem.

You do not need to own a robot or operate a laboratory to contribute a demonstration. But collecting the movement is only the beginning. The data must still be processed into a format that training systems can use.

That is why an @axisrobotics  task is more than clicking until a scene looks correct

You are helping create a machine-readable example of how a task should be performed.

The public Axis technical report and repositories show this broader direction across browser infrastructure, trajectory cleaning, task generation and model training.

I wrote a complete beginner guide explaining how to complete and sign your first Axis contribution.

The real question is no longer:

“Can humans control a robot?”

It is:

“Can thousands of people produce enough clean, diverse and verifiable demonstrations to help robots operate in the real world?”
